chapter: Jazz and society in New Orleans
title: Her society newspaper work and decades of debutante parties
summary: She worked the society beat on and off for about thirty years and says Black bands stayed most popular at debuts, including for her 20-year-old daughter's generation.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: you said you were a member of the press, you were doing the society work, I think.

Yes, I had been several years before I was married, then I was married. I resigned, and then they needed someone temporarily, and I went back, and of course, on the news paper, it's very hard to get away from it, and I stayed and stayed.
How long have you been doing this?

Well, 30 years off and on, but I wouldn't, a great many of those years I haven't been on. More recently, I was on five years, so it has given me the opportunity through these years to have kept up pretty much with activities, even though it was past the age when I would have been going to debutante parties. So you have
been going to debutante parties every year?

Except during the war, I'd say when I was away most of the time, and I sometimes I went from the newspaper to cover it for pictures and things, and then sometimes friends of mine, their daughters would make their debut and I would go, and it seems to me the most popular form of music all through these years has been ambience and colored bands. Wouldn't you say?
I don't know about through the years, but you'd say that through the years it's maintained in it.
I would definitely say that. speaking for myself and speaking for all of my contemporaries and my daughter's contemporaries and through the ages, all the groups I've ever had to deal with.
You'd say your daughter's contemporary is like it too? Oh,
And how old is your daughter?
